h: פָּרָשַׁת זָכוֹר, מַאֲמָר ז׳ Parshas Zachor — Maamar Zayin

p: To what may the matter be compared? etc.
This one you mentioned and that one you mentioned;
over a bowl full of every good thing,
and that one over an empty bowl.
So too, regarding Shabbos it is written,
and regarding Amalek it is written, 'Remember…
that they said to Moshe Rabbeinu,
it is stated in the Mechilta
but you shall count in the name of Shabbos."
That is, "the first day toward Shabbos,"
"second day toward Shabbos," and the like.
And the essence of the holiness of Shabbos
only by virtue of the remembering
in thought and in speech beforehand.
Now the remembering of Amalek too
only in thought and in speech alone,
will "you shall erase…" be in actual deed.
only to bring up into the memory of the mind,
perhaps, just as through the remembering
of the holiness of Shabbos in thought alone
there is thereby drawn and poured forth
of the deed of Amalek in thought
there could be drawn into the soul
as it says, "who happened upon you on the way";
and it is stated in Tanchuma (Teitzei 9)
as in the matter of which it says (Devarim 23:11),
אֲשֶׁר לֹא יִהְיֶה טָהוֹר מִקְּרֵה לַיְלָה
'who will not be pure because of a nocturnal occurrence';
he made you cold as water,
as in the matter of which it says (Mishlei 25:25),
And it is stated in the Mechilta
beneath the wings of the Cloud
And in Tanchuma (Teitzei 10) and the Pesikta (ibid.)
it is stated that Amalek had no dominion
except over one whom the Cloud had expelled.
what they said in the Mechilta,
from beneath the wings of the Cloud:
אִם הָיָה לוֹ כֹּחַ לִכְנוֹס לְשָׁם
if he had the power to enter there,
he could have killed them there;
Also, the precision of its wording:
It will be understood according to
what our Sages of blessed memory said
כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת לֹא הָיָה לוֹ כֹּחַ
for in truth he had no power
but by introducing into their thoughts
עַל יְדֵי זֶה הָיָה גּוֹנֵב הַנְּפָשׁוֹת
thereby he would steal the souls,
so that they became defiled by a nocturnal occurrence.
And this is why they said specifically "souls,"
for I did not muse by day
so as to come to impurity at night."
And so automatically the Cloud expelled them, as mentioned above,
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה הָיָה לוֹ כֹּחַ לְהוֹרְגָם
and thereby he had the power to kill them.
And this too is the allusion:
אֲשֶׁר לֹא יִהְיֶה טָהוֹר מִקְּרֵה לַיְלָה.
"who will not be pure because of a nocturnal occurrence."
to defile the souls through their thoughts
even while they were within the holiness
beneath the wings of the Cloud,
"Amalek dwells in the land of the Negev":
that is the power of the evil inclination
from the side of the serpent;
and he dwells in "the land of the Negev" —
in a soul that is dried out
from all the desires and lusts of this world.
And specifically against such a soul
"and against Torah scholars more than all."
And this is the power of the primordial serpent,
to put the thought of lust into their hearts,
and that it was a delight to the eyes."
And also according to the one who says
and made you cold as water,"
הוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ אָמְרָם זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה
it is along the lines of the statement of our Sages of blessed memory
on the verse "Do not trust a companion,
do not rely on a friend" (Michah 7:5):
"If the evil inclination says to you,
'Sin, and the Holy One, Blessed is He, will forgive,'
as it says, 'Do not trust a companion' —
וְאֵין אַלּוּף אֶלָּא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
and 'aluf' means none other than the Holy One, Blessed is He,
שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר [יִרְמְיָה ג, ד] אַלּוּף נְעוּרַי אָתָּה.
as it says (Yirmiyah 3:4), 'You are the guide of my youth.'"
His Name, may He be blessed, by the term "aluf" —
that this is the essential scheme of the evil inclination:
to put into a person's mind
that all the warnings and punishments
are only to frighten and threaten a person,
like a father who trains his son from his youth,
so that he will walk on the straight path,
אֲבָל בְּוַדַּאי לֹא יַעֲנִישׁ בְּנוֹ חֲבִיבוֹ
but certainly will not punish his beloved son
even if he transgresses his command.
And this is why they called Him by the name "aluf,"
כְּמָה דְּאַתְּ אָמֵר אַלּוּף נְעוּרַי אָתָּה
as it says, "You are the guide of my youth,"
וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר אַל תַּאֲמִינוּ וְגוֹמֵר
And about this it says, "Do not trust…,
do not rely on a friend."
And this too is the power of Amalek:
he made you cold as water":
that there is no need to be
This too is among the enticements of the serpent,
for it was only to threaten and frighten you;
Hashem's whole intent is to frighten you
so that you not know of good and evil,
He will not punish you with death.
And on this matter we have indeed spoken,
regarding what they said in the holy Zohar
"And in all that I have said
that is to say: I have warned you sternly
concerning the word of My service;
take heed, so that there not come upon you
But according to this it should have said,
"And from all that I have said to you, take heed" —
from all the threats and punishments,
that they not come upon you.
And we said that it hints
that specifically through the threats and the punishments,
"in all that I have said to you" —
through that you will be guarded.
And this is juxtaposed to the Shabbos of Shemittah,
the fear of Hashem will be upon your faces,
and automatically they will be guarded from all evil
and will fulfill their duty through the fear of the threat
and maamar 6; see there at length).
But Heaven forbid to rely on this
and to make the punishments light in one's eyes,
as is the counsel of the evil inclination and Amalek,
שֶׁעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר אַל תַּאֲמִינוּ בְּרֵעַ.
about which it says, "Do not trust a companion;
do not rely on a friend," as mentioned above.
וְלַאֲשֶׁר כֹּחַ עֲמָלֵק גָּדוֹל כָּל כָּךְ
Now since the power of Amalek is so great
to defile and confuse the thought
in the two aspects mentioned above,
אוּלַי עַל יְדֵי זְכִירָה שֶׁלּוֹ בַּמַּחֲשָׁבָה
that perhaps through remembering him in thought
there would cling to them, Heaven forbid,
some trace of musing from his side,
and perhaps it would further spoil
אֶת כֹּחַ הַזְּכִירָה דִּקְדוּשַּׁת שַׁבָּת כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל.
the power of the remembering of the holiness of Shabbos, as mentioned above.
And to this replied to them
Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him,
on the intent of the person's remembering,
as in the parable: "This one I mentioned
over a bowl full of every good thing" —
הַיְינוּ עַל יְדֵי כַּוָּנַת הַזְּכִירָה שֶׁל שַׁבָּת
that is, through the intent of the remembering of Shabbos,
this is in essence brought about:
And through the remembering of Amalek,
that his memory is erased from the soul.
And in Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer (ibid.) the wording is:
"A cup of spiced wine is not like
this is a cup and that is a cup;
this is 'Remember' to keep and to sanctify, etc.,
and that is 'Remember' to destroy, etc."
It appears that no special intent at all is needed
as in the parable of the two cups,
between which there is no distinction
to the sight of the human eye;
and likewise regarding the two rememberings,
one need only fulfill both with simplicity
according to His command, may He be blessed,
and Hashem will complete it on our behalf:
that through the remembering of Shabbos
holiness will flow into the soul,
and through the remembering of Amalek
his memory will be erased from the soul
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר תִּמְחֶה אֶת זֵכֶר עֲמָלֵק
as it says, "You shall erase the memory of Amalek

paragraphs.text: Mekhilta DeRabbi Yishmael, Bachodesh 7:9 — “Rabbi Isaac says: Do not count in the manner in which others count; rather, count for the sake of Shabbat.” The days of the week are numbered in relation to Shabbat. Rav Tzadok reads this habitual naming as preparation of thought and speech before the day arrives.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Ki Teitzei 9 — “Rabbi Judah says: ‘He encountered you’—he made you impure, as it says, ‘who is not pure because of an occurrence at night.’ Rabbi Nehemiah says: He actually called you. ... He stood outside the cloud and called to them: Reuben, Shimon, and Levi, come out, for I am your brother and wish to do business with you. When they came out, they killed them.” The Midrash records distinct interpretations of the same word. Rav Tzadok develops the interpretation of impurity as an inward attack on thought.

paragraphs.text: Mekhilta DeRabbi Yishmael, Amalek 1:2 — “Rabbi Elazar of Modiin says: ‘Amalek came’—because Amalek would enter beneath the wings of the cloud, steal souls from Israel, and kill them, as it is said, ‘He encountered you on the way and struck all your stragglers behind you, when you were weary and exhausted, and did not fear God.’” The unusual phrase “steal souls” is in the original Mekhilta. Rav Tzadok interprets it as corrupting thought in a way that removes a person from the cloud’s protection.

paragraphs.text: Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer 44:3 — “The pillar of cloud surrounded Israel’s camp like a walled city, and no adversary or enemy could reach them. But anyone who needed immersion was expelled by the cloud outside Israel’s camp, which was holy; Amalek would strike and kill those behind the cloud.” This gives the stated condition under which Amalek could reach those separated from the protected camp.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Rabbeinu Bachya on Devarim 23:10 — “‘Guard yourself from every evil thing’: that a person not think by day and come to impurity at night; therefore it is juxtaposed with ‘a man who is not pure from a night occurrence.’” The pasuk Rav Tzadok uses for “karcha” stands in the Torah’s laws of the camp going out to war. So the defense of Yisrael’s camp is the purity of daytime thought, the very point Amalek attacked to draw souls out from under the cloud.

paragraphs.text: Chullin 37b:6 — “‘Behold, my soul has not been defiled’—I did not entertain thoughts by day that would bring me to impurity by night. ‘I have not eaten carrion or torn flesh from my youth’—I never ate the flesh of an animal hurried to slaughter because it was dying. ‘No rejected meat entered my mouth’—I did not eat from an animal concerning which a sage had to issue a ruling.” The first interpretation directly links thought by day with the nocturnal impurity used in Rav Tzadok’s account.

paragraphs.text: Sukkah 52a:10 — “‘For he has done greatly’—Abaye said: Against Torah scholars more than against everyone else.” The preceding interpretation identifies the passage as the activity of the evil inclination: it set its eyes on the Temples and destroyed them and their scholars. Superior attainment does not remove the need for vigilance.

paragraphs.text: Chagigah 16a:15–16 — “Rabbi Judah son of Rabbi Nahmani, the interpreter of Resh Lakish, expounded: What is meant by ‘Do not trust a companion; do not rely on an intimate’? If the evil inclination says to you, Sin and the Holy One, blessed be He, will forgive, do not believe it. ... ‘Companion’ means the evil inclination, as it is said, ‘The inclination of the human heart is evil’; and ‘intimate’ means the Holy One, as it is said, ‘You are the intimate of my youth.’ If you say, Who testifies against me? The stones and beams of a person’s house testify against him.” Rav Tzadok explains the temptation as falsely treating divine warnings as threats that will never be acted upon.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Ki Savo 8 — “‘Af ki amar Elokim’ — what does it matter that God said it… Amalek’s kelipah is to cool a person so that he not care so much for Hashem’s command.” There Rav Tzadok draws the consequence: while this cooling remains, Torah and mitzvos cannot be done in full love and fear, so the Name (Yud-Hei with Vav-Hei) is not whole.

paragraphs.text: Zohar II 123b, Mishpatim 23:1 — “‘In everything I said to you, take care.’ What is meant by tishameru? Should it not say tishmoru? Rather, tishameru certainly. What is ‘that I said to you’? That is: that I warned you concerning the word of My service. You will be guarded, so that no evil reaches you. You will be guarded through that keeping and protection of Mine alone.” The original distinguishes the active command to observe from the passive promise of being protected. Rav Tzadok explains how the warnings themselves awaken the fear that protects.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: R. Moshe Chaim Luzzatto, Mesillas Yesharim, ch. 4, discussion of justice and mercy — “To remove from the hearts of those who wish to be deceived the thought that the blessed Master will not bring small matters into His judgments or reckon with them, the rule is: ‘Whoever says that the Holy One overlooks wrongdoing—let his innards be forfeit.’ They likewise said: ‘If the evil inclination tells you, ‘Sin, and the Holy One will forgive you,’ do not listen.’ … The measure of mercy sustains the world, which could not stand at all without it; nevertheless, the measure of justice is not impaired. … But the measure of mercy grants the opposite of the three things we mentioned: the sinner is given time rather than being cut off immediately when he sins; the punishment itself does not utterly consume him; and repentance is granted to sinners as a complete kindness, so that uprooting the will is reckoned as uprooting the deed. … This is certainly a kindness beyond strict justice, yet it does not wholly contradict justice, since there is a basis upon which it can rest.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Ramchal specifies what divine mercy actually changes: time, the measure of punishment, and the availability of repentance. This sharpens Rav Tzadok’s distinction between warnings that preserve a person through fear and the inclination’s false inference that those warnings are empty and may safely be ignored.

paragraphs.text: Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer 44:10 — “Israel said to him: Moses our teacher, one verse says, ‘Remember what Amalek did to you,’ and another verse says, ‘Remember the Shabbat day to sanctify it.’ How can both stand? He answered them: A cup of spiced wine is not like a cup of vinegar. This is a cup and that is a cup. This is remembering in order to observe and sanctify the Shabbat day; that is remembering in order to destroy and cut off all the seed of Amalek.” The analogy compares identical vessels with opposite contents. Rav Tzadok draws from it the power of fulfilling both commands in simplicity.
